content: In the physical sciences, an intensive property, also referred to as a bulk property, is a physical characteristic of a system that remains independent of the system's size or the quantity of material within it. In contrast, an extensive property of a system is directly dependent on the system's size or the amount of material it contains. For example, viscosity is an intensive property, but it is an empirical macroscopic quantity and is not applicable to extremely small systems. An intensive quantity, also known as an intensive variable, is a physical quantity whose value does not depend on the amount of the substance being measured. This is in contrast to an extensive quantity. For instance, the mass of an object is not an intensive quantity because it depends on the amount of the substance being measured. However, density is an intensive property of a substance. A classic example of confusion between intensive and extensive properties is the riddle, What weighs more, a pound of feathers or a pound of lead? This highlights the distinction between the two types of properties. To describe any thermodynamic system, at least one intensive property and one extensive property are required. If a set of parameters, denoted as {a_i}, are intensive quantities, and another set, {A_j}, are extensive quantities, then a function F({a_i}, {A_j}) is an intensive quantity if it remains invariant under scaling of the extensive parameters. For example, the ratio of two extensive quantities results in an intensive quantity. For instance, density (an intensive property) is calculated as mass (an extensive property) divided by volume (another extensive property). When two systems or substances are combined without interaction, the resulting intensive variable is a weighted mean of the individual intensive variables. For example, in a thermodynamic system composed of two monatomic ideal gases, if the gases are mixed, the final temperature is a weighted mean based on the number of particles in each gas and their respective temperatures. This demonstrates that intensive variables are independent of the total amount of the system, provided other influencing variables remain constant. Examples of intensive properties include temperature, pressure, chemical potential, density, viscosity, velocity, electric field, electrical resistivity, spectral absorption maxima (in solutions), and specific energy. An extensive quantity, on the other hand, is a physical quantity whose value is proportional to the size of the system it describes. Such a property can be expressed as the sum of the quantities for the individual subsystems that make up the entire system. Extensive quantities are the counterparts of intensive quantities, which are intrinsic to a particular subsystem and remain constant regardless of size. Dividing one type of extensive quantity by another typically yields an intensive quantity. For example, dividing mass by volume gives density. If a set of parameters {a_i} are intensive quantities and another set {A_j} are extensive quantities, then a function F({a_i}, {A_j}) is an extensive quantity if it scales proportionally with the extensive parameters. Extensive quantities are homogeneous functions of degree 1 with respect to the extensive parameters. This relationship is consistent with Euler's homogeneous function theorem, which states that the partial derivative of an extensive function with respect to an extensive parameter, while keeping all other parameters constant, is also extensive. Examples of extensive properties include mass, length, volume, entropy, enthalpy, energy, electrical resistance, texture, and heat. Certain perceptions are often described or measured as if they are intensive or extensive physical properties, but perceptions are fundamentally different from physical properties. For example, the color of a solution is not a physical property. A solution of potassium permanganate may appear pink, various shades of purple, or black, depending on its concentration and the length of the optical path through it. The perceived color of a sample (e.g., its degree of pinkness or purpleness) cannot be measured directly but can only be ranked in comparison to other colored solutions by a panel of observers. Attempts to quantify a perception always involve an observer's response, and biological variability is an intrinsic part of the process for many perceived properties. For instance, a given volume of permanganate solution at a specific concentration has physical properties related to its color: the optical absorption spectrum is an extensive property, while the positions of the absorption maxima (which are relatively independent of concentration) are intensive properties. A specific absorption spectrum will always be perceived as the same color by a given observer, but different absorption spectra may be perceived as the same color. Thus, there is no precise one-to-one correspondence between an absorption spectrum and a perceived color, even for the same observer. The confusion between perception and physical properties is further compounded by the existence of numerical scales for many perceived qualities. However, this is not measurement in the same sense as in physics and chemistry. A numerical value for a perception represents the expected response of a group of observers when perceiving a specified physical event. Examples of perceptions related to intensive physical properties include: Temperature: All observers will agree on which of two objects is hotter. Loudness of sound: The related physical property is sound pressure level. Observers may disagree about the relative loudness of sounds with different acoustic spectra. Hue of a solution: The related physical property is the position of the spectral absorption maximum (or maxima).
